speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to make a statement regarding the final payment on 1954-55 wheat pool operations. On May 3 I advised the house that the Canadian wheat board was making a cut-off as at May 4 covering the 1954-55 wheat pool account, and that I would be in a position at about this time to announce to the house the amount of the final payment and the rate per bushel for each grade of wheat delivered to the pool by producers.
Producers' deliveries of wheat to the pool were 318-4 million bushels. A total of 164-1 million bushels, including 42 [DOT] 9 million bushels of sales contracts, were transferred to the 1954-55 pool from the 1953-54 pool as at April 29, 1955. Deliveries from other than producers amounted to 600,000 bushels, bringing the total volume of wheat in the pool to 483 [DOT] 1 million bushels. Completed sales to the close of business on May 4 amounted to 321-7 million bushels. Therefore there remained as at May 4 a balance of 161-4 million bushels. These stocks included 112 million bushels covered by sales contracts and unsold stocks of 49 -4 million bushels.
In closing out the 1954-55 pool the sales contracts were transferred to the 1955-56 pool at contract prices and unsold stocks were transferred on the basis of board selling prices for May 4. The final operating surplus in the 1954-55 pool is $62,588,000 from which must be deducted the interim payment made earlier this year. This payment amounted to $22,261,000. After providing for P.F.A.A. levy on the interim and final payments and after allowing for final payment expenses, the surplus for distribution to producers as a final payment is $39,680,000.
On producers' deliveries of 318-4 million
bushels the average final payment is 12-461 cents per bushel.
The final net payments to producers on the principal grades of wheat are as follows:
No. 1 northern, 14-815 cents per bushel.
No. 2 northern, 15-143 cents per bushel.

speechtext:
In view of the questions that have been asked with regard to the seamen's strike on the great lakes, Mr. Speaker, I might bring the house up to date with the situation. The terms of settlement of the dispute between the seafarers' international union and the association of lake carriers were agreed to in discussions between the parties and the mediator, Mr. Goldenberg, at an early hour this morning. But because of a new development in the situation an adjournment was taken until three p.m. today to give the mediator and the representatives of the parties some rest. During the past few days conferences have been going on almost continuously.
The new development to which I refer arose out of the fact that there are two other unions, representing deck and engine room officers respectively, involved in disputes with the same employers, and while they are not jointly carrying on negotiations with the seafarers' union and the employers' association there is a tacit agreement between the three unions to support each other, and representatives of the two officers' unions have been present as observers at the conferences presided over by the mediator.
The disputes between the two officers' unions and the employers have not yet gone through the conciliation procedures provided by our legislation but it is the desire of all the parties concerned that a settlement be reached at the present time resolving all three disputes in order to avoid the possibility of another work stoppage at a later date involving the ships' officers.
It is to this problem that Mr. Goldenberg, the mediator, has to address himself this afternoon and I have every confidence that he will be as successful in this endeavour as he was in the other.

speechtext: The house resumed, from Thursday, May 17, consideration of the motion of Mr. Howe (Port Arthur) for the second reading of Bill No. 298, to establish the Northern Ontario Pipe Line Crown Corporation, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Diefenbaker, and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Coldwell.

subtopic: CONSTITUTION OF CROWN COMPANY TO CONSTRUCT PIPE LINE, MAKE SHORT-TERM LOANS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I understand I have nine minutes left which I wish to use in summing up my remarks of last night. In order to do that I wish to say that early delay and the necessity now for speeding up to meet the deadline of June 7 can be explained on the ground that it was necessary to make certain no vested interests in gas are created on the United States side of the line which would rob this country of supplies of gas and transfer control south of the border.
Once the government had decided it was necessary to keep at least three hundred million cubic feet of gas on this side of the line, it would have been absolutely foolish for the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) to have been running to council with proposals to take from 400 to 500 million cubic feet of gas out of this country.
The government, for the same reason Sir John A. decided to build a trans-Canada railway, decided to build a trans-Canada pipe line, or to have a trans-Canada pipe line built. To build a line to Winnipeg without making sure there was an all-Canadian connecting link between the prairies and the industrial east would have resulted in building a line south to market gas. This would not only have drained a source of power out of Canada but would have drained the young men and women out of the part of the country which needs increased population, not decreased population. Population certainly would follow a gas line into every industrial centre from Emerson through Minneapolis, Milwaukee, Chicago and Detroit, and vested interests would have taken control of the gas entirely out of the hands of Canada.
The C.C.F. say, "We agree with all that but let the government build the line". We point out there are fields in which government ownership is essential. We prove it by the success of hydroelectric power put in by Conservatives in Ontario and telephones and

power put in by Liberals in Saskatchewan, but we point out that the present Saskatchewan government has proven, when they attempted to apply the principle of public ownership and control generally, that it has its limitations.
We recognize that under private enterprise there must be legitimate profits and sufficient risk must be taken out of any national project to make legitimate profits possible before it can be financed.
Now therefore we join with Ontario to build the bridge across northern Ontario just as we paid $7 million to bridge the freight costs over the same area. But benefiting from the experience of Saskatchewan we encourage private enterprise to develop a billion dollar development in Alberta and eastern Canada. There is provision in the bill to allow private enterprise to take over the whole project if that is found feasible, but there is also provision to bring the whole line under the government if that is necessary to retain both the line and control on the Canadian side of the line.
It is not bad for United States capital to come in here from a friendly nation any more than it was bad for United States independence that British capital came in from an unfriendly nation in the early stages of United States development. It would have been bad to get quick sale for Alberta gas to the United States which would have created vested interests in the United States and drained our population south. This plan protects Canadian interests in every possible way and permits the entrance of United States capital into the development of our industry in a manner which increases friendship and wards off enmity.
Mr. Manning of Alberta, Mr. Campbell of Manitoba and Mr. Frost of Ontario say that time is of the essence. The hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) speaking for the Conservatives, and numerous C.C.F. members from the west, have boasted, one to ward off United States domination and the other to bring in socialism, that they are going to use every device possible to prevent this measure going through.
They have used every possible device which the rules permit them to delay the bill. They have delayed estimates by talking, they have prevented debate and have wasted time by calling a total of 15 votes within the last week. They have used every device the rules of the house permit to delay the passing of this measure. We are using the one device available to us, and it is a device the Tories gave us in 1912, by making closure possible. They have used it four times; we may have to use it four times. They have compelled us to do this. We are simply using a rule they gave
Northern Ontario Pipe Line Corporation us to overcome their use of the rules. They could have discussed this matter for 15 days if they had not followed the procedure they have been following of avoiding discussing it at every opportunity they could. By using the rules of this house they have deprived themselves of the right to discuss the bill. They have deprived themselves of the right to discuss a pipe line across this country. Yesterday the hon. member for Prince Albert denied a member of his own caucus the right to get up and put him right on something he was stating to this house. They are following every possible device to delay things with regard to this matter and to prevent it getting before the people of Canada and have to date succeeded fairly well in wasting most of the time that has been made available to them.
In summing up what I had to say last night with regard to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) who is in charge of the measure may I say that as I look across at my C.C.F. friends I realize that close to a majority of them were born outside of this country. When I look at my friends immediately across the aisle I remember that one of their ablest members, the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe), was born down there. In view of the fact that I had my elementary education in the United States, although I was born in this country, I am beginning to think that we are not a bad bunch of people. Although there may have been early influences on our lives down in the United States, since we have become members of this house we have done nothing but try to serve the best interests of the people of Canada and, as I said last night, the Minister of Trade and Commerce has been a leader among us.

There are also those on the maritime seaboard, on the Atlantic coast, who will reap no benefits.
I am interested to note that the title given to the bill, namely, an act to establish Northern Ontario Pipe Line Crown Corporation, is far more realistic than the grandiose name chosen by the company which will obtain the loan and the greatest benefit from this crown corporation when it is set up. Just fancy, this company has the audacity to call itself Trans-Canada Pipe Lines! Trans-Canada indeed! Why, there will be no pipe of this company laid within a thousand miles of my constituency. Yet it calls itself Trans-Canada Pipe Lines. We should like to examine this all-Canadian pipe line and to see whether it is worth our while investing the money that they will take from our people in taxes. In 1951, five years ago, Mr. Tolmie came down here representing the trans-Canada pipe line company and he put forward the argument that this was a simple proposition, that there might be some little difficulties and some lean years-three lean years, in fact-after they had the pipe line constructed until such time as they had built up the market in eastern Canada. At that time there was no reference whatever to the necessity of exporting any gas. The markets would soon be available in eastern Canada. There would be only three tough years, according to him, and the only interest he had was to build
[Mr. Pearkes.}

a pipe line across Canada to bring Alberta gas to what he described as fuel-hungry parts of eastern Canada. With those representations, it was not unreasonable that the government, feeling that it would be an excellent thing to have a pipe line in Canada rather than for the gas to be sent across to the United States, agreed and gave a franchise to this company to go ahead.
Then it became evident to the company that it would be necessary to export some of the gas to the United States. A proposition was made that two-fifths of the daily amount of gas passing through the pipe line could easily be spared and could be exported with advantage to the United States. It was said it would be better to do that south of Winnipeg rather than send it directly south from the gas fields of Alberta. A branch line was to be built from Winnipeg to Emerson and through that branch line there would be some 200 million cubic feet passing daily. Reasonable-yes; we will authorize that.
Then, they had to look for a distributing agency in the United States and this chosen instrument of the government selected the Tennessee Gas Transmission Company to be the importing and distributing agency in the United States. But then difficulties were encountered because there is a law in the United States, a very reasonable law, that any organization importing gas into the United States must obtain a permit from the federal power commission. Nobody could take any objection to that, so an application was made to the federal power commission to see whether 200 million cubic feet a day might not be imported into the United States. Proceedings were held before this commission, and the commission had certain responsibilities to the other distributing agencies in the United States. It soon became evident that if the Tennessee Gas Transmission Company imported gas into the states immediately south of Manitoba, they would be conflicting with other companies such as Northern Natural Gas; People's Gas and Coke and American Louisiana, distributing companies already in that area or with projects already laid out for the distribution of their supplies into the area into which Tennessee was entering.
They made strong representations to the commission, and as they were powerful companies there was every indication that the proceedings would be very, very long. Of course, there are other interests too. There are the coal mining interests in the United States who have been selling their coal to Ontario for many years. They do not want to lose that lucrative market, so they are also making their representations to the federal power commission. There was no likelihood

in the immediate future of the Trans-Canada company being able to get enough money from their exports to the United States to construct the portion of their line between Winnipeg and Toronto around the north shore of lake Superior.
It was then desirable to re-organize the finances of the company to see whether, by bringing in other powerful interests, other high class salesmen, they might not be able to interest United States and Canadian investors in this company. They must raise the money somehow if they were going to build this pipe line. But the Canadian and United States investor was not interested. He was not at all sure that this would be a paying proposition if, by any chance, Tennessee was not able to import and sell the gas in the United States. He was not at all sure there would be a market even for the 300 million cubic feet per day in eastern Canada. I do not know whether any consumers have already declared their intention to buy the gas in eastern Canada. Anyway, there was a great deal of uncertainty and the public was not going to fall for it. So the company came to the government again and said, "Will you construct this difficult portion of the line around lake Superior?" The government, anxious to fulfil their promises, agreed to construct this line between the Manitoba boundary and Kapuskasing, together with the Ontario government, for something over 118 million.
Then what happened? I think you begin to see the sinister workings that there are behind this whole scheme. Trans-Canada Pipe Lines company got a corner on all the available pipe and the pipe is safely stored in the yards of the United States manufacturers on the other side of the border where the Canadian government cannot get hold of it and where no other Canadian company could possibly reach it. It is under guard on the other side of the border. They have cornered all the pipe that is available, all the pipe that is required.
Then, what happened? They came back to the Canadian government to say, "If you want that pipe line built this year or next year, we are the only people who can do it; we are the only people who have got the pipe." Now, then, hand out another $80 million, and the poor little Prime Minister and "UNO Who" crept down into the barrel, scraped the bottom of it and handed out to the blackmailers another $80 million. Mr. Speaker, I think that these transactions are worthy of Horatio Bottomley. If you remember, Horatio Bottom-ley during the first world war, who under the guise of being a patriot, fleeced the British people of millions of their money. Oh, he was
Northern Ontario Pipe Line Corporation quite a character. He had a very attractive personality, so attractive that although he had robbed the small British middle class people, he could still come back to them and with a smile they handed out their money again. Oh, he was quite a sportsman. He kept a string of race horses and he used to breakfast every morning on kippers and champagne. I do not know whether the Prime Minister breakfasts on kippers and champagne, but there are certain characteristics which are not dissimilar between Horatio Bottomley and the present government. Horatio Bottomley ran a newspaper, you may recall, entitled John Bull. Signs were posted up all across the United Kingdom during the first war: "If you see it in John Bull it is so". That is akin to the propaganda which is now being put out by this government: "If we say it is so, it is so". There is no need to ask any further questions. Must it be done this year? Remember, I am speaking for people who have to help pay for this line and are going to get no benefit from it. Must it be done this year? That gas, that oil in Alberta, has been there for centuries. Fifty years ago, when I first came out to this country,-and I was born in another country; I was not born in this country, but I have been here for over 50 years-I saw the gas coming out of the ground in Medicine Hat and the flame burning. It has been there all those years. It seems to me that Toronto has been a big industrial city for a long time and they have got on very well without this Alberta gas. Oh, if it is really necessary, let us know. Why is it so imperative that it must be started this year? Are all those factories around Chicago in desperate need of this gas this year? They can get gas from other directions. Is Fort William so urgently in need of gas? Is northern Ontario? Are the people going to freeze to death there? They have been living in that district for a very long time.
What about Winnipeg? I have lived in Winnipeg. We did not have any gas then and everybody seemed perfectly happy. I passed through some of the defence establishments within the last few months. I noticed great piles of coal and elaborate and excellent heating arrangements for the burning of that coal at Rivers, at Shilo, at Fort Osborne barracks. Is it necessary to change all this coal heating apparatus over to the burning of gas right away? No, I do not think so. I cannot see the urgency of this proposal. I think it would be much better-and I am quite

From time to time in this house we have heard various arguments advanced and pious hopes expressed regarding the decentralization of industry. I would in that case permit the hon. member for Vancouver South to appeal to the people on behalf of Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited and I shall tell the people about anti-Canada pipe lines limited.
In the time at my disposal I intend to show that we need a survey of Canada's resources in the matter of energy that is available and may be made available. We need a survey of the needs of Canada during the next 25 years as far as energy and power are concerned. Until such an analysis has been made on a national scale I feel it is not correct for the government to take from the public purse hundreds of millions of dollars for a scheme that is looked upon in many responsible circles as a doubtful scheme at best. The very fact that private enterprise seems unwilling to risk its capital in what is usually a most lucrative enterprise should give us cause for serious consideration.
I mean to argue in support of public ownership of the line, if a line is necessary. I maintain that this entire proposal is solidly against the national interest. I feel that even the agreements which have been entered into by the minister with Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited are not agreements to which any responsible businessman in Canada would apply his signature. The agreements are so one-sided and full of loopholes that the public interest is not being looked after.
I said I felt a survey of Canada's energy resources and requirements is badly needed. We have atomic energy rapidly developing. We do not know and we are not being told what role atomic energy is likely to play within the next 25 years. Many of these vast expenditures we are making may be entirely unwarranted and unnecessary. We need to be told what is taking place and what we have reason to expect. A survey should be made of our coal resources. In the interests

of all those who need coal, the people of Canada as well as the people who mine the coal, consideration must be given to what is the future role of that fuel. We have huge resources in British Columbia, Alberta and Saskatchewan and also in the maritime provinces. What is the future of oil in supplying the energy needs of the Canadian people? What future is there for hydroelectric energy and, finally, what is the picture in relation to natural gas? We need to know what supplies there are of these energy producing resources. We should know how much we need, what are the best and most economical means of transporting energy to where it is needed, what is the relationship of these resources to unemployment, what is the relationship of our energy resources to national development, the decentralization of industry, methods of distribution and what should be the role of private enterprise versus public enterprise. We should know what is the future role of atomic energy, what should be our policy with regard to the export and import of fuels, what must be done to preserve our heritage, what conservation measures are necessary, what is the relationship of the production of energy to irrigation and how it relates to our future population. Some study should be given to price structure, measures of government control and the subject of taxation.
I feel the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) has often rendered a service to this country in emphasizing the need for the early setting up of a national fuel policy board that will have its fingers on such problems as I have outlined. It is scarcely good enough that we are continuing to pursue the matter in this haphazard fashion whereby individuals, and foreigners at that, move about the country and look at where they can make a rich grab with little regard for the consequences to the people of Canada and the future welfare of this country.
There is much to be said for public ownership, Mr. Speaker. The most convincing argument for it in this case is that the people are going to pay for the line in any event. The minister is now offering to build the western leg and to entirely own the northern Ontario section. If the people have to pay for it by means of taxation, the people have a right to claim ownership. I have never before heard of someone having to pay for something and not being able to claim possession of that for which he has paid.
The Ontario and Saskatchewan governments are on record as being in favour of public ownership. Manitoba has its publicly owned hydro system and I am sure the province would not be averse to entering into an agreement whereby it also might
Northern Ontario Pipe Line Corporation become a shareholder in this public enterprise. There is plenty of evidence on the record that the Alberta government is most anxious to sell gas and I am convinced that is their desire. Judging from the letter of the premier of Alberta which the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) put on the record yesterday, the government of that province is anxious to sell gas. The last paragraph of that letter reads in part as follows:
.	. . we feel your government would be fully
justified in taking whatever steps are necessary.
I think that indicates how anxious the Alberta government is to get rid of its gas.
There are other advantages to public ownership. Public ownership allows proper conservation measures to be exercised and it allows for distribution in the national interests. If private enterprise owns the line it will build the line where and when it can make the most money. It will build the line only to such places as will provide it with the greatest revenue. No consideration whatever is given to the national needs. On the other hand, public ownership allows for the equalization of rates to consumers in smaller communities with those in larger communities. Private enterprise will not even bother servicing smaller communities because there is no money in it for them. They simply want to service areas where there is mass consumption.
As has already been pointed out by my colleagues, public ownership will mean lower capitalization costs and can ensure that the national heritage of the people will be preserved.
Private enterprise means the establishing of a monopoly. It is our contention that when a monopoly exists, whether through necessity or otherwise, that monopoly should be subject to public ownership and in this case to direct public ownership. I feel direct public ownership would give the government a splendid opportunity to aid the lower levels of government, in that many municipal governments would be able to undertake their own distribution and thereby relieve taxation on real estate in their municipalities. That situation exists in the case of hydro. In many municipalities in Canada the local government is able to relieve taxation by looking after its own hydro distribution.
I feel the present proposals are unacceptable to the people and against the national interest. The taxpayers are asked to run the risk and if the thing turns out to be an uneconomic venture the taxpayers of Canada will have lost hundreds of millions of dollars. If it is not a paying proposition Trans-Canada will never buy that northern Ontario
4076	HOUSE OF
Northern Ontario Pipe Line Corporation section; it will be a white elephant on the hands of the taxpayers of Canada. If there is money in this northern Ontario section the company will be pleased to buy it and reap the profits. The people have everything to lose and nothing to gain. It is not in the national interest because control over one of our basic natural resources is being handed over to foreigners.
The export of energy may be vital to our development. We should have a policy whereby we will export only surplus energy and not energy vitally necessary for our national development.
By and large the bill is a poor bill. It sets out a poor policy because it gives almost unlimited power to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe). He can tear up these agreements next week and sign new ones. Many Canadian people may have the utmost confidence in the present Minister of Trade and Commerce but I would point out that one agreement is for a 25-year period. I certainly hope that the minister will be hale and hearty and living in retirement in beautiful Burnaby 25 years from now, but I certainly do not believe he will still be Minister of Trade and Commerce at that time. Regardless of the confidence Liberals may have in the minister's integrity, it should be borne in mind that this legislation may be administered in some future year by a Conservative, a C.C.F. or even a Social Credit Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Liberals in this house may yet regret that they wrote out a blank cheque to the Minister of Trade and Commerce.
The management of Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited have no personal stake whatever in this operation. I am not at all surprised that Mr. Tanner saw fit to resign as a cabinet minister in the Social Credit government of Alberta. By buying only two shares in Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited he is given the management of hundreds of millions of dollars of the taxpayers' money which is being handed over by a grateful federal Minister of Trade and Commerce. This is certainly a good deal for Mr. Tanner, much more lucrative than any cabinet position in the province of Alberta.
I am given further faith in my theory that this proposal is unacceptable to the Canadian people by the fact that large sections of Canada will have to pay for this pipe line without getting anything out of it. The people of British Columbia are having to pay for their own pipe line in the price they pay for gas delivered by Westcoast Transmission, and why should they be called upon to pay
[Mr. Regier.l

for a pipe line to serve other provinces of Canada? We feel that that is a double imposition upon them.
If this is to be a trans-Canada pipe line in fact and not just in name, it should include in its set-up the line now being built by West-coast Transmission so that we could also reap benefit from the taxes that Canadians in other parts of Canada will have to pay.
I wonder what the miners down in Nova Scotia will think of this bill. When this gas arrives in Montreal it will throw them out on the streets. The Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) has always refused to accept responsibility for the unemployed. Those miners will be thrown out on the streets and yet they will have to pay taxes for the very thing that is causing their unemployment. I cannot see the Liberals winning many seats in mining areas in Canada.
The limitation of $130 million in the bill upon the amount which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) can lend the crown corporation means that it will be financially impossible for the corporation to build the Ontario section or even begin to build it until the company has repaid the loan in connection with the western link. That also is not in the public interest. If we are going to start building a pipe line we should be starting to build the whole pipe line, not just the western link.
Much has been made of the need of United States capital in Canada. A lot of people who know little of economics have been making some rather wild statements. They have been saying that Canadian national development will be seriously handicapped if United States capital does not continue to enter Canada in the large amounts in which it is presently coming to this country. That is an absolute falsehood as less than 10 per cent of our overall investment in 1956 is dependent upon United States investment. To even argue that we could not curtail our expansion program by 10 per cent is most ridiculous, especially as it is expected that our capital investment program will be 20 per cent greater this year than last.
The agreements themselves constitute a piece of bad business. First of all, the bill is a blank cheque. Then I notice the minister's method of doing business. I have a copy of the agreement between the government of Canada and the government of Ontario. The government entered into the agreement with Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited on November 21 to arrange for the section through northern Ontario, yet it was not until the day after that Mr. Porter of the government of Ontario signed a letter agreeing to the terms

of the contract for the northern Ontario section. In other words, the minister went out on a limb; he ran the risk of this agreement not being sanctioned by the government of Ontario at the time he signed it. I think that is an indication of how he does things. The "great C.D." is a quotation we often hear, but we find that he makes agreements by telephone or otherwise and signs his name on the dotted line before he has the sanction to do so by the government of Ontario.
The agreement provides for the gift of the line by whoever may be Minister of Trade and Commerce to Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited. In a period of about 15 years, if the line is found to be a paying proposition, the Minister of Trade and Commerce will have the right, if he so wishes, to sell the northern section to Trans-Canada Pipe Lines for the sum of $1. The agreement provides for that. The agreement says that the minister may charge 70 per cent of the original capital cost as defined in the agreement; the company has no right to purchase unless it is willing to pay 70 per cent of the capital cost. However, there is nothing in the agreement to stop a federal minister of trade and commerce selling this line to the company for the sum of $1. I submit that that should be remedied before any federal government builds this pipe line.
I fail to understand the logic of insisting on an interest rate of 3J per cent on our investment in connection with the northern Ontario section. This is a 25-year deal, this is long-term money which usually carries a higher rate than short-term money, but this government turns around and offers a shortterm loan at an interest rate of 5 per cent. I see no logic in that. There is no financial logic whatsoever in that type of deal. We are satisfied to let them have money for 25 years at 3J per cent but on the other hand when we give them a loan for ten months we insist on 5 per cent.
The first agreement regarding the northern Ontario section is already a dead agreement because the company has already violated it in many respects as to dates of ^meeting obligations. The company is also-this is another serious loophole in that agreement -under no obligation to use the pipe line at all. They can allow the government to build the pipe line and they may use it but they do not have to use it. It may be a white elephant from the very day it is completed. If this company is going to build a larger pipe line south of the border which it will own I see no reason why it should want to use the government pipe line and have to pay a high rental on it.
Northern Ontario Pipe Line Corporation
The agreement with regard to the western section allows the minister to make a maximum loan of $80 million. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris), however, may lend to the corporation $130 million. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) created the impression that if the government had to take over the company because the company defaulted the shareholders and investors would lose money. There is nothing in the agreement to assure the taxpayers of that. The agreement says that the minister may buy the shares and he may even buy options on shares. He may take over the assets and rights of the company if it defaults in its payments but he may also take over all the undertakings of the company. In "undertakings" we can safely include the undertakings that the company has with respect to its shareholders. In other words, if the government needs to take over the company at the end of the ten months or at the expiry date of the loan there is no assurance to the Canadian people that the scandalous deal by which the shareholders and stockholders of all the bankrupt railway companies of Canada were bailed out by a government and the C.N.R. loaded with a terrific and unnecessary capital overhead will not once again be repeated and we will have a similar shemozzle.
When the minister takes over Trans-Canada he even has the power to pay back to them the $15 million he says they have already spent. I am wondering how much of the $15 million was a contribution to the Liberal campaign fund in 1953. There is nothing to block Trans-Canada Pipe Lines from making another heavy contribution to the next Liberal federal election campaign, and there is nothing to stop the Minister of Trade and Commerce from assuming all the indebtedness of the company with the taxpayers' money. I feel that these agreements have far too many loopholes to be sanctioned by any responsible minister of the government.
Much has been said about the C.C.F. being in an unholy alliance with the Conservative party on this subject. My reaction to that is that we of the Conservative and C.C.F. parties are Canadians all and Canadians first. The Conservatives may well represent only the monied class, the huge industrialists of Canada and what have you. I shall fight the Conservative party on their own ground at the proper time. However, so far as this problem is concerned I recognize the loyalty of my political opponents when I see it, and I have never yet accused the Conservatives of not being, as well as the C.C.F., a loyal and honest Canadian political party. The day will come when we will have in Canada

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, facing the realities of the situation as it now exists in Canada and the position of government and political parties that a northern Ontario route for the first gas pipe line east from Alberta has top priority, then the government's present proposal for assistance to Trans-Canada offers the fastest, lowest cost means of getting the project under way. I support it for that reason, and for that reason alone. Let me therefore very briefly outline the main arguments which have been used against the plan by its opponents in this house and among Canada's press. Because some of the same arguments come from various sources I will name no particular source, but merely try as best I can reasonably to answer the arguments.
The summary, sir, might well be called "fable versus facts". Some may disagree that what I call facts are such and argue also that what I may call fable is indeed fact. Whether they be members of this house or editors, I think Canada's public has every reason to expect some reasoned and accurate rebuttal from them on the specific points I will mention rather than vague generalities and loose charges and damnation of Americans, of which there has been so much.
The first fable, Mr. Speaker, that I should like to mention is the claim that Americans are going to get natural gas at bargain prices while Canadians will pay more. The facts, sir, are these. With load factors and the type of gas sale taken on the same basis as between Canadian and American customers of Trans-Canada, sales over the border will actually be at the same, or slightly higher, prices to the Americans than to Canadian customers in the same area. To be specific, Manitoba is the nearest Canadian market area to the point of export at Emerson. As to customers in Manitoba communities taking gas at 100 per cent load factor-by "100 per cent load factor" I simply mean taking gas at exactly the same maximum volume every
4082	HOUSE OF
Northern Ontario Pipe Line Corporation day of each year-under the existing contracts those customers big and small in Manitoba will for 25 years get a flat price of 26-2 cents per thousand cubic feet. The sale to Tennessee Gas Transmission Company at Emerson for resale in the United States at the same 100 per cent load factor involves an average price payable during the 25 years of that contract of 27-07 cents per thousand cubic feet if the volume of gas sold is 200 million feet a day; or would increase to 28-73 cents a thousand feet if the total volume exported were 400 million feet a day. This indicates, sir, a difference in favour of the Manitoba consumer at this particular load factor rate of at least one cent per thousand feet differential favouring the Canadian customers. I might say that the same approximate difference in favour of the Canadian customer in Manitoba carries through under the existing contract at any other load factor condition of sale you want to take into account. Later in my remarks I will place on the record the specific details of the various contracts entered into by Trans-Canada, both in Canada and with American customers.
Now, the other form of sale to the United States that is involved is the sale of excess gas; that is, gas that cannot be sold during the summer months to any Canadian customer in Ontario or Quebec. This is to be sold, if it is available, at Niagara to Tennessee for storage during the summer in Pennsylvania storage fields. This will be sold at a price comparable to the central Ontario prices for summer interruptible gas supply, which is now under contracts already entered into priced at 33 cents to 34 cents per thousand feet.
The next fable that I want to deal with, sir, is that the McMahon plan would involve the sale at Emerson to the United States at prices from 5 cents to 7 cents per thousand cubic feet higher than the prices under the present Tennessee plan. The facts are simply these. McMahon claims that he can get about 30 cents per thousand feet for up to 400 million cubic feet daily at a 90 per cent load factor for a 25-year period. This remains to be proved; for a vague offer is not a firm contract. Even, however, if his price could be validated by signed contracts it would be only one-quarter of one cent per thousand feet higher than Tennessee's average price under its firm contract, which would be on the basis of 90 per cent load factor 400 million feet a day sale, 291 cents per thousand feet under the price escalation contract covering the next 25-year period.
The third fable, sir, is that Trans-Canada would not be under Canadian control. The facts in answer to that are simply these. No matter who owns shares, any pipe line com-


pany in Canada is always under most adequate government control in our own country. At the producing end of the pipe line governments of producing provinces have complete authority over the volumes, prices, equitable market sharing among gas well owners, and so forth, related to gas supply for the pipe line system, whether that pipe line markets its gas in that producing province only, in Canada only, or internationally. Provincial authorities in the consuming provinces through such bodies as the Ontario fuel board, the Alberta public utilities board and similar organizations in other provinces, have full control over rates, charges to consumers by gas distributors, over the rates of earnings permitted distributors, thus providing strong provincial check-reins over gas transmission companies as well as contracts with the distributors in each of those provinces. The federal government has complete control over the transmission company no matter who owns it and regulates not only the rate of earnings that company can make-of course it does not guarantee the company against loss-but also has full control at all times over export or import permits, including the terms of volume and price involved in contracts for which export permits or import permits are required.
The fourth fable, sir, is that Canadians will not be given a chance to invest in a large way on fair terms in this proposed Trans-Canada pipe line. The facts again are simply these. When public financing becomes feasible, which it is not now, Canadians can buy at least 51 per cent of the total issued capital of Trans-Canada at comparable prices to the present cost of stock held by the current shareholders, but without taking the heavy risk which is now involved for the present shareholders of that company.
The fifth fable, sir, is that there is not even any assurance that Canadians will constitute a majority of the directors of the board of Trans-Canada. Trans-Canada, sir, is a special act company incorporated by an act of parliament and that act prescribes that the company is bound by section 155 of the revised Companies Act of 1934. That section, sir, reads as follows:
No person shall be elected as a director unless he is a shareholder owning shares absolutely in his own right, and not in arrear in respect of any call thereon; and the majority of the directors of the company so chosen shall, at all times, be persons resident in Canada, and subjects of Her Majesty, by birth or naturalization.
Therefore, Trans-Canada, regardless again of who may have the majority of shares, must at all times comply with section 155 of Canada's own Companies Act and have a majority of its directors both residents of Canada and subjects of Her Majesty.

Now, I might say, sir, of the present board of Trans-Canada of some 17 men, 10 of them are Canadians. I think all 10 are men who will be regarded by most thinking Canadians as pretty solid citizens. I am going to mention their names and their locations because I think it would be most unfair to have these types of Canadians unfairly labelled, as the company has been, as being made up of "Texas buccaneers" or some other such thing.
The 10 Canadian directors of Trans-Canada are: N. E. Tanner, Calgary; Hon. Edouard Asselin, Montreal; E. W. Bickle, Toronto; M. A. MacPherson, Regina; J. K. McCausland, Toronto; H. R. Milner, Edmonton; A. D. Nesbitt, Montreal; G. P. Osier, Winnipeg; Jules R. Timmins, Montreal; and J. Ross Tolmie, Ottawa.
Mr. Speaker, the next fable is that the proposed federal-Ontario government northern Ontario Crown Pipeline, for lease under purchase option to Trans-Canada, is a subsidy or handout to the Trans-Canada shareholders.
I think the facts can be described in this way. Trans-Canada will gain a major deferment of carrying charges during the early tough years of market build-up in Ontario or Quebec, but these deferred charges become a first charge against profits of the over-all Trans-Canada system when it reaches a profit position. The actual net saving to Trans-Canada will be an average annual interest saving of about $1,250,000 for the years until the Crown Pipeline is purchased by Trans-Canada, at depreciated value plus 3i per cent annual interest, plus depreciation.
Even this is not a handout to Trans-Canada shareholders, but rather a cost saving to Canadian gas consumers. The Northern Ontario bridge plan has been taken into account in recent reductions in sales contract prices to Canadian distributors. These price reductions, with Ontario the principal beneficiary, will amount to over $2,500,000 annual savings to Canadian consumers during the early years and progressively larger annual savings as consumption expands in eastern Ontario.
To give you a specific example of the type of savings which will result to eastern Canadian consumers specifically as a result of this bridge plan of government assistance, also aided by the proposed sale of gas at Emerson, Manitoba, I would like to quote the contract price proposed two years ago in the H. K. Ferguson (Shattuck) report to the board of transport commissioners in June 1954. At that stage, which was prior to the contemplation of any government assistance, the average weighted price for gas to be sold in the province of Ontario to all types of consumers was placed at 51i cents per thousand cubic feet. As a result of various measures of export and government assistance the new
Northern Ontario Pipe Line Corporation contract prices in Ontario work out to an average weighted price of 46-6 cents per thousand cubic feet, a saving of 4-9 cents in the weighted average cost. This saving has made a world of difference in the extreme difficulty of distributors in competing with other fuels and their ability to successfully compete with natural gas at competitive prices. The same type of comparison could also be made for other provinces.
The next fable is that the proposed $75 to $80 million loan to Trans-Canada to cover 90 per cent of cost of the 1956 pipe line from Alberta to Winnipeg is a handout to the company or a subsidy. The fact, sir, is that this is a short term, 9-month loan at a full commercial interest rate of 5 per cent. Security for it is the pipe line itself which will cost $7 to $8 million more to build than the amount of the government loan, and will be worth an additional $7 million based on expected higher steel, freight and labour costs if construction is delayed beyond this year. The other assets of Trans-Canada, including rights of way, engineering, purchase and sales contracts, et cetera, which represent a multimillion dollar investment, are also security for the government. Should the government have to foreclose next spring owing to the inability of Trans-Canada to complete its quarter billion dollar financing program, the government will receive an operating pipe line and a start on an Alberta to Quebec pipe line system at a bargain price.
The next fable is that the government will make a handout of up to $200 million to Trans-Canada. The fact is, sir, that that argument is as phony as a $3 bill. First, no handout is involved at all. Second, the Winnipeg line loan would be fully repaid before Ottawa and Ontario start the northern Ontario pipe line section and the federal government's share of that would likely be under $100 million; thus there will not be more than $100 million of federal money involved at any time, and no part of that is a handout or subsidy.
The next fable is that somebody other than Trans-Canada could build a pipe line this year and the fact, sir, is that no private company, no matter who backs it, could be organized, get the necessary government permit, gas purchase and sales contracts, engineering, rights of way, finances or pipe in less than two years; nor could any crown company, even if the federal government was willing to commit itself to a capital expenditure of some $400 million. Nor could it be done if by some miracle, Quebec, Ontario, Manitoba, Saskatchewan or Alberta could be quickly persuaded to join in such a venture.

The next fable, sir, is that there is no urgency for a start on construction this year. The facts are that the governments of Alberta, Manitoba and Ontario and the government of Canada all say that a start is urgent. So, too, say the Alberta producers who have already made a tremendous $150 million investment and have been hog-tied mainly by politics for several years. Common sense also dictates urgency, for the costs of pipe, labour, and freight are going higher, reducing the economics of the project. Actual pipe line construction is needed to spur a United States decision in favour of gas import from Canada.
The final point indicating the urgency of a start is the long delayed development in the prairie provinces of a great by-products industry based on the by-products of gas, and the petrochemical plants, sulphur plants and other industries and the population boost in the west that will accompany these plants. All of these things are urgently needed in the west. The sooner dry gas can get into the market the sooner will the west have new plants of many kinds using the byproducts of that gas, employing many thousands of Canadians and paving the way for a much broader and sounder economy in that part of Canada.
The next fable is that Trans-Canada would syphon off gas to the United States to the detriment of eastern Canadian consumers, and the government investment in the northern Ontario pipe line. The fact is that there are several reasons this could not possibly happen. First, the federal government has control over the volume and terms of export at all times. Second, the company will initially have about $175 million of private capital invested in the pipe line system east of Winnipeg, over and above the government investment in northern Ontario, and the huge private investment can only bring earnings if large volumes-as much as can be sold- are moved into eastern Canada through the system. The third reason is that the government-owned section leased to Trans-Canada involves as part of rental payments a first charge on profits of the entire Trans-Canada system. Thus any failure by the company to get maximum markets in eastern Canada by diverting gas south of the border from Manitoba would result in the Northern Ontario Pipe Line Crown Corporation draining off Trans-Canada's export profits as rental payments on the government "bridge" pipe line.
The fourth reason, sir, why we need not fear the draining off of gas to the United States is the vast size of the present shut-in gas reserves in Alberta and the huge rate at which this surplus is expanding. This

Obviously this government decided that it would go in for a bigger and better give-away program than had ever been conceived. It decided that not only would the prize be much bigger, but the question would be much easier.
These are the questions you must answer to qualify. First: Are you a corporation which is predominantly owned by foreign interests? If you can answer "Yes" to that question, the second question is: Have you defaulted on your undertaking which was the basis for your being awarded a government franchise? If you have answered those two questions correctly, this government will do almost anything to bail you out of any financial difficulty you might run into, or build your whole project for you.
However, if you happen to be a Canadian province, for example Saskatchewan, and apply to the federal government for assistance to build a dam which will irrigate half a million acres of farm land, and provide you with enough hydroelectric power to industrialize your province and increase the standard of living of your people, then you know of course that you are going to be turned down flat.
Or if you happen to be another Canadian provincial government-for instance the government of New Brunswick-and you happen to be applying to this government for federal backing for your power development bonds which, if granted, will not cost the federal taxpayer or the federal government one penny, but will simply make it possible for you to borrow the money you need to build your project at a great deal lower rate of interest, and thus save your taxpayers millions of dollars a year, then, Mr. Speaker, of course you know that once again you are out of luck, and that you can count on being turned down flat.
It has become fairly obvious, Mr. Speaker, that if you want to get anywhere with this government, you must first of all be a foreign-owned corporation and, second, have the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) wrapped around your little finger. If you happen to qualify on both those scores, then you know that the sky is the limit and that there is absolutely nothing that this government will not do for you.
Let us have a look at this legislation, Mr. Speaker, and see what it will do. First of all, 67509-259
Northern Ontario Pipe Line Corporation it will provide 90 per cent of the capital to build the first third of the line. Then it will provide 100 per cent of the capital to build the second third of the line. So, by simple arithmetic, we find that this government is providing 95 per cent of the capital to build this whole line.
Up until a year ago, this chosen instrument of the government, this Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited, professed over and over again its ability and intention to build the whole line unassisted by the government. Then suddenly, a year ago, the company came to the Minister of Trade and Commerce, cried on his shoulder, and professed inability to finance construction. Of course, without question,- it being his chosen instrument-the Minister of Trade and Commerce did exactly what the company wanted him to do. He believed everything they said; did not question them in any way; and agreed to build the northern Ontario section of the line for the company. He did it, of course, with the money provided by the taxpayers of Canada.
Then, spurred on by that initial success, a little while ago Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited again came to the minister; again cried on his shoulder and said, "We cannot finance the building of the prairie section of the line". Once again the minister listened to everything they said; believed it without question- because, after all, it is his chosen instrument, it is his baby; the company cannot do anything wrong in the eyes of the minister-and agreed to give them everything they asked for. He agreed to put up 90 per cent of the cost of building even the easiest section of the line.
The worrying part about this matter,-bad though it is so far-is that there is no doubt about it that when this line reaches Kapus-kasing, Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited may be counted on once again-spurred on by those two initial successes; after all, it has been so easy, why not try it again?-to come to the minister and cry on his shoulder a third time; and as he did without question on the first two occasions, he will say, "Certainly; if you want it, I will finance the construction of the remainder of the line". Hence we shall see this whole line built by the government.
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) made an amusing statement this morning. He said that the Conservative party objected to United States capital coming into Canada to build this pipe line. Mr. Speaker, we do not object to United States capital coming into Canada to build this line. We object to the fact that there is no United States capital coming in to build this line. We object to the fact that the capital is to be provided just about 100 per cent by the Canadian taxpayers,

What is the reaction of the people of Canada, Mr. Speaker, to the expenditure of public funds in order to enable United States interests to take over the transportation and marketing of a large proportion of one of our vitally important natural resources? The answer to that question was given by a nation-wide Gallup poll which reported as follows on May 2 last. I quote from the official report of the Gallup poll:
45 per cent of the people of Canada favour a pipe line built and run by private Canadian investments.
29 per cent favour a line built, financed and administered by the government.
17 per cent favour a line built partly by the government and partly by private investments from Canada and the United States.
8 per cent had no opinion.
One per cent gave various and sundry other answers.
Of the 17 per cent who favoured a line built partly by government and partly by private interests, more than half opposed this proposal if it meant the possibility of American control.
It is therefore clear that, because Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited is owned and controlled 83-4 per cent by foreign interests, only 8 per cent of the people of Canada are in favour of the present government plan for building this line. That leads us to the logical question: Why should a policy that is favoured by less than one out of every twelve Canadians be thrust down the throats of the Canadian people? It is simply because one man, namely the Minister of Trade and Commerce, is determined to have his way. This is the same man, the same minister, who a year ago was determined that parliament should grant him unlimited and unchecked power. That power was denied him for one reason and one reason only. That reason was that the Conservative party was determined that no minister and no government should be granted power of that kind. Today, Mr. Speaker, the Conservative party is just as determined that this minister and this government shall not impose their will on the overwhelming majority of Canadians who oppose this legislation.

Three years ago this house passed a bill to incorporate a company known as Niagara Gas Transmission Limited. Hon. members will perhaps recall that that bill had a stormy passage. It was eventually arranged that Trans-Canada Pipe Lines would build a pipe line from Niagara to Toronto, importing gas from the United States which would temporarily relieve a gas shortage in eastern Canada and serve to build up eastern markets for western gas. This was a temporary alleviation of the power requirements of Ontario and Quebec. I want to emphasize that it was only temporary because, power being the vital key that it is, no thinking person can rely on having this power permanently delivered from another country.
Northern Ontario Pipe Line Corporation
Mr. Frost realizes that this is only temporary, but the Conservative party under the leadership of the present Leader of the Opposition ignores this temporary feature. Eastern Canada can wait for one, two, three or perhaps four years for western gas without being hurt, but let us look at the position of western Canada. A large percentage of this gas is being burned daily because of a lack of markets. There is no pipe line to carry it away. This is a waste of a precious asset, and every day it continues to go to waste is an unhappy day in Canada's history.
Over and above the amount which is being wasted is the development which is being held up by the lack of markets, and this is tremendous. Southern Saskatchewan is hungry for power, and there is no pipe line to bring temporary power from the United States to southern Saskatchewan. In Winnipeg a Winnipeg gas company has already gone to great lengths in preparing for the arrival of this gas. That city is hungry for this power, and there is no pipe line built so the city of Winnipeg can get temporary gas.
This applies in a greater degree to that wasp waist of Canada north of the great lakes where they are less favoured as regards power than are other parts of Canada. They have all kinds of resources there in the pre-Cambrian shield, but they have not the power with which to develop those resources. At the present time there is no pipe line to bring them gas temporarily from the United States and thus serve those communities. Yet the official opposition in this house will smugly say that western Canada can wait. Is it any wonder that holding such views that party has reached the present low ebb?
The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill) referred yesterday to the pipe line which was originally proposed to carry gas from the Alberta fields to Winnipeg and then south to the border, and which was later united with the first Trans-Canada gas company. Northern Ontario Pipe Line Corporation is best served by serving the welfare of all Canada. They have never demonstrated it more convincingly than on this occasion, when they have dragged their loyal western supporters into such an indefensible position.
The hon. member for Calgary South (Mr. Nickle) is the only one who has taken what could be described as a normal Conservative position on this issue. In the final analysis there is only one issue: Is the pipe line to be built by private enterprise, or are we to rely entirely on public ownership? This is a time when the Tories should be saying, "Me too," and saying it honestly. The Canadian people would have given them full marks for saying it.
In his speech on the resolution the hon. member for Calgary South stated most emphatically that he was out and out for private enterprise based wholly on economics, without allowing any margin for national considerations which might arise because of the economics of the bridging time necessary to build up eastern markets until the line across north of the lakes could be completed. He was always for exporting as much gas as possible to the western United States. Fortunately our nation was not built on that philosophy. However, the hon. member has always been consistent. He knows and he has stated that delay at this time would cost far more than the cost of the northern Ontario section. This in itself indicates the measly cost of this northern Ontario section when placed against the value to the nation of the whole project.
Canada is developing at a more rapid rate than any 15 million people have ever developed in all history. They will need this power which is stored beneath the western prairies for their continued development. 1 do not say they should not export any of it to the United States, but I do say they should be cautious and examine carefully any export of something so vital to their future. Canada has demonstrated before that she recognizes obligations beyond her boundaries and that 15 million people cannot sit on treasures of the magnitude of our Canadian treasures with a dog in the manger attitude, but we must scrutinize carefully the export of power.
This attitude has always been taken by all governments in this country, and it has been taken also by the United States. That is the reason so much time is being taken in

scrutinizing the power question by the United States federal power commission, which has delayed this project up to the present time.
Last night the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) gave some figures on gas- this was for the benefit of the C.C.F. party-and power in cities in Saskatchewan. I do not have time to go into why these costs are so high. I shall leave that for C.C.F. speakers, but I should like to say that in Edmonton the lowest rate, which of course is a commercial rate, is 17 cents per thousand cubic feet. When the amount used is from 10,000 to 42,000 cubic feet per day the rate, and this is still a commercial rate, goes up to 19 cents per thousand cubic feet. The domestic rate is 25 cents. These figures are vastly different from those we heard the Minister of Agriculture give with respect to that socialist province right beside the province of Alberta.
As I said earlier in my address, there is only one real issue at this time and that is public ownership versus private ownership. Assuming that we could get all the pipe needed and that all other things were available that are not available from other companies, I want to give the reasons why we cannot afford the luxury of public ownership in this instance. We have already heard that the gross national product of Canada this year will be somewhere between $26 billion and $28 billion. The Minister of Trade and Commerce has already announced that it is estimated that capital expenditures in Canada this year will be $7J billion. This is a record percentage for any nation at any time, and I do not exclude Russia.
Serious doubts have been expressed as to the ability of our economy to find the goods and services to accomplish this capital expenditure. This means that there is danger of serious inflationary pressures within our economy. Canada is fortunate in being next door to the United States so these inflationary pressures may be cushioned by spilling over into their much larger economy. The mechanics of this spilling over involve the importation at such a time of United States capital for development.
I am one of those who have constantly urged the maximum rate of development for our country, with particular emphasis on the Canadian northwest; and since 1 have so constantly urged the maximum rate of development I again want to say that I support as strongly as I am able the procuring of the wherewithal to expedite this rapid development. When our own resources are being used to the maximum extent, we must do all possible to encourage the importation of outside capital. This outside capital is

not just paper money; this outside capital is orders on goods and services from beyond our borders.
In the case of the proposed pipe line the outside capital which we hope will go toward its construction will be orders for pipe of various sizes, heavy construction machinery, and the know-how of citizens of another country. These are things we lack, and we are grateful to be able to procure them for our benefit. If the line were publicly owned we would have to obtain these things with Canadian dollars. Canadian dollars are not orders on goods in another country, and we would have to purchase United States dollars to obtain these goods and services. At this time this would add further inflationary pressures, and if we insisted on carrying on this project without that outside capital the rate of our development would have to be slowed down.
Since the pipe line is vital, the government has indicated that it will be built as a public ownership project if necessary, which is proper; but if it became necessary to accept this proposition it would be with heavy hearts on the part of those who are most anxious for development. However, I have every confidence that it will not become necessary. I want to see United States capital come into our country, and having said that I want to put this idea on the record; that from personal observation I have noticed that not only people immigrate to a country but capital immigrates in the same way. A satisfactory share of the United States capital that has come into our country in the past has become nationalized as Canadian capital, and a satisfactory share of the United States capital that is coming into our country in the oil and gas fields will become Canadian capital. Whatever rewards we as Canadians must pay for the capital that enables us to develop our country, will be paid willingly and I hope with an expression of gratitude to those who are willing to express their confidence in us.
We have done a great deal about our own development but it has not all come about because of our own efforts. We have received assistance from others. However, I am pleased to say that having been assisted we have justified that assistance by continuing our development more and more through our own efforts. In proportion to our gross national product the use of outside capital is diminishing. Our gross national product is rising at a very great rate, and while more and more outside capital is coming into the country the ratio between the two is lower and will continue to diminish.

I feel that the issue is the one which was pointed out just a few minutes ago by the hon. member for Churchill. The issue is whether this will be a private enterprise or whether it will be a public enterprise. I, together with my colleagues in the C.C.F. party, feel it is essential that this be a public undertaking, so the Canadian consumers of gas will not be fleeced by a monopoly in that field.
As far as I am concerned I am not blaming or casting reflections upon the people of Trans-Canada Pipe Lines or others who perhaps may be interested, on a private basis, in constructing this line. I think it is somewhat unfair to charge those people with having ulterior motives. I think it is up to this government to decide how much private enterprise and how much public enterprise we should have in this country. I think it is up to the elected representatives of this country to decide where private enterprise and where public enterprise fit into the economic plan of this country.
I for one support those who have suggested that here is a program for the transmission of gas from the fields of Alberta through to Winnipeg, as proposed under this plan, which should be under public control.


The plan is, of course, to extend that pipe line from the vicinity of Winnipeg. While nothing is said at the present time about the 110-mile line from the vicinity of Winnipeg to the Ontario-Manitoba border, I expect that once again this Liberal government will come to this house and ask for more public money to finance this 110 miles of pipe line. In addition, there is no question about it that the Canadian public will be obliged to put up the money, in the initial stages at least, to build the long pipe line through Ontario to Toronto. Hence I say that here is an issue that is of utmost importance to this house and to every Canadian citizen, namely whether or not we should at this time launch upon the proposal put forward by the minister and the government to put in the hands of United States investors the right to control the transmission of gas to the various consuming centres in this country. I say that it is a sell-out of one of the most important natural resources in this country.

Right Hon. C. D. Howe made a spirited defence of the government's pipe-line policy in parliament, but analysis of his arguments reveals them to be self-defeating. He says that gas is only one of several competing heat and energy sources, and it would not be in the public interest for the government to subsidize gas transmission and provide unfair competition to coal and oil producers.

This company, the Ogdensburg bridge authority, was incorporated by a special act of the parliament of Canada in 1952 for the purpose of building a bridge from Prescott, Ontario, to Ogdensburg, New York. At the time the act was introduced the best estimate of the cost of the bridge was in the neighbourhood of $10 million to $12 million. As a result of this estimate which, of course, was necessarily based on incomplete information, the right of the company to issue debentures was limited to $10 million under section 16 and $12 million under sections 12 and 17.
Since the company was incorporated plans for the construction of the bridge have been prepared and more complete engineering data have been obtained, with the result that it now appears that the cost of the bridge will be at least $15 million. I might mention the fact that the legislature of the state of New York has just approved a bill authorizing the sum of $15 million to be lent to the company to be secured by debentures and to be used in the construction of this particular bridge. In an abundance of caution, and to ensure that the principals will not have to return to parliament for a further amendment after the commencement of construction, this

He said: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of the bill is to obtain authority to build a bridge over the St. Lawrence river between two points, one on the north shore above Three Rivers and the other on the south shore below Nicolet. As the bill concerns my riding, which is 100 per cent French in origin, I intend to give my explanation in French, which before this house has equal standing with the English language, the learning of which I enjoyed very much.
(Translation) :
Mr. Speaker, before dealing with the bill now before the house, I should like to give a bit of history.
The proposed bridge will serve two very important districts, that of Three Rivers and that of Nicolet.
Historically speaking, the city of Three Rivers is one of the oldest in Canada. It was the second one to be founded after Quebec. Originally it was a fur trading post. That trade led two men from Three Rivers, following their expeditions into the far north and into the Hudson bay area, to go to London and set up, with British capital, even under the French regime, the Hudson's Bay Company which contributed to the development of the far north and the Canadian northwest.
Later, Three Rivers was the site of the first iron working industry, under the French regime. Everyone has heard of the Three Rivers ironworks. As everyone knows, iron developments in the province of Quebec are getting more and more important; it was at Three Rivers that a powerful ironworks industry was born and its memory is perpetuated by one of the Canadian Iron Foundry plants.
Later on, the city of Three Rivers became a railway centre and one of the main pulp wood centres of Canada. Today, its mills are among the largest and most important in the country.
Around Three Rivers, such cities as Cap-de-la-Madeleine, Grand-Mere, Shawinigan and La Tuque, have developed, and all are located in central Quebec.
Now, on crossing the river to the south shore, we find the county of Nicolet, which also dates back to the early days of colonizafMr. Boisvert.]
tion; it has always been a wholly agricultural district. However, at one time there was a little seaport there known as Port St. Francois, operated by a company located at Sherbrooke, with an office in London. For many years, immigrants from England landed at Port St. Frangois. This sea port has now disappeared following the construction of highways and of a railway line.
On the south shore, the district serves and will continue to serve Victoriaville, Thetford Mines, Richmond, Sherbrooke, Drummond-ville, St. Hyacinthe and Sorel. Therefore, we readily see the importance of connecting the two shores of the St. Lawrence river at the points I indicated a few moments ago in English, that is one on the north shore a little above the city of Three Rivers and the other on the south side, some ten miles below the town of Nicolet.
We hope, for the county of Nicolet, that the Imperial Oil Company, which for many years has made explorations for gas and oil, will eventually make borings to a greater depth and find such research profitable.
We also look forward to the day when the little port of St. Francois, which has played an important part in the historical development of our province, will be able to resume its former activities. The channel on the St. Lawrence river is but a few hundred feet from the bank and there is there a site ideally located for the establishment of a sea port.
The construction of that bridge is urgently needed. In fact, last year, almost a million pedestrians and 400,000 vehicles had to take the ferry boats, in the middle of the summer and in extremely difficult conditions, to cross the river.
When this bridge is built, it will connect the eastern townships, the county of Nicolet and the'city of Three Rivers with the American boundary, which is only 120 miles away from this town, apart from the fact that construction of a highway between the important harbour of Portland, on the coast of Maine, and Three Rivers, will make this a shortcut from the United States to the heart of Quebec.
The bridge is to be built by a private company. It will be 5,000 feet long and will cost almost 15 million dollars. It will be a toll-bridge, but experts who have studied the project are in no way worried about the future of this bridge, and claim that even now they are sure to obtain the required building capital. The structure is a necessity

for the local farmers whom I represent, and also for the development of the city of Three Rivers. Sixty per cent of the food products brought into Three Rivers come from the county of Nicolet-Yamaska and, thanks to this bridge, farmers will certainly benefit considerably.
Hon. members know that it is generally not possible to build a bridge in a province. Within a province, bridges, like highways and railways, are recognized to be under provincial jurisdiction. When a bridge is to be built on the St. Lawrence river, under chapter 140 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, no permit may be awarded unless an act is passed by parliament, authorizing the construction of this bridge over the navigable waters of the St. Lawrence. This hill aims at obtaining this permit. According to plans already prepared, the arches of the bridge will have to be high enough not to impede navigation, and plans thereof must be approved by the governor in council.
We are confident that, if this legislation is passed, the Three Rivers and Nicolet area will be provided with a highly modern bridge that will facilitate the heavy traffic which, especially in the summer months, goes through that area which is at the very heart of Quebec and, in addition, is one of the finest of the province.
Three Rivers is half way between Montreal and Quebec city on the north shore, while Nicolet is half way between Montreal and Quebec city on the south shore.
The Three Rivers harbour is increasingly important. It ranks fifth for the volume of shipping and the bridge will only serve to increase its traffic. In my opinion, the reasons I have given in the course of my explanation-I could give a thousand more if it were necessary-warrant the passing of the bill now before the house.
