speakeroldname: Mr. Stanley Knowles (Winnipeg North Centre) moved
speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND HOURS OF POLLING
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 205, to amend the Canada Elections Act (hours of polling).
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am grateful to the house for agreeing to the substitution of my name as the sponsor of this bill which was introduced and given first reading on Monday, March 19, by our late friend and colleague, Mr. J. W. Noseworthy. As hon. members will realize, the bill seeks to make a very simple change in the Canada Elections Act, but we feel it is one of those changes that are desirable. The proposal is simply that with respect to by-elections that happen to be called during the period of the year when daylight saving time is not in effect the polls should not close until seven o'clock in the evening.
The situation with regard to general elections seems to have taken care of itself so far as the problem raised by this bill is concerned. The reason I say that situation seems to have taken care of itself arises from the fact that six out of the last seven general elections in Canada have been held during the period when daylight saving time is normally in effect. There are in the papers once again today rumours about the next election.

Canada Elections Act
As a matter of fact, rumours of that kind are quite common around here, and I think it is to be noted that everyone seems to expect the election to be held next year, and everyone expects that it will take place during the time of year when daylight saving time is in effect. In fact the general expectation now seems to be that it will take place on June 17, 1957.
However, may I point out what happens so far as general elections are concerned with respect to employees who are at work and have to take advantage of section 47 of the Canada Elections Act regarding time off for voting. Section 47 makes a slightly different provision than was in effect for quite a number of years. As hon. members will recall, the elections act used to provide that every employee had to be given two hours off on election day for purposes of voting. Many difficulties arose, difficulties of interpretation, as to what was meant by that two-hour clause. That ambiguity and uncertainty were cleared up to some extent when the provision was changed to read as it now does that every employee must have three clear hours during the time the polls are open in which he can vote.
It is clear from the provisions of section 47 now that if an employee has three consecutive hours of his own time during the period that the polls are open he does not get any time off work; but if he does not have three clear consecutive hours his employer has to give him whatever time is necessary so the total time he will be off while the polls are open adds up to three hours. Thus, if the polls close at six o'clock and an employee would normally get off work at five o'clock it is considered that he has one hour of his own time. The employer has to give him another two hours. If there are cases where the employee is at work during the whole of the period that the polls are open, of course he has to be given three consecutive hours by his employer. Any such time off has to be given without loss of pay.
Now, with general elections taking place during the period of the year when daylight saving time is in effect in most parts of Canada, the pattern is reasonably satisfactory. There are always complaints about these matters, but I think it is correct to say that the pattern is reasonably satisfactory in that during the period when daylight saving time is in effect the election is still run on standard time. Therefore the requirement that the polls close at six o'clock standard time turns out to be seven o'clock daylight saving time. Accordingly, that means that for most employees it is simply a matter of being let off, under the provisions of section 47, at four o'clock.

Now, there are a great many factories, shops and stores where five o'clock, or 4.30' o'clock, is the normal closing time. Perhaps five o'clock is more general than 4.30 o'clock but, at any rate, in the cases of shops and stores where the normal closing time is five o'clock all the employer has to do is let his employees go at four o'clock so those employees have the three clear hours between four o'clock and seven o'clock.
I suppose that in reciting this picture I am conscious of the fact that that is what obtains to a very large extent in my own constituency, indeed in the city of Winnipeg as a whole. For example, the railway shops which employ a large number of workers in the city of Winnipeg have accepted it now as pretty routine practice that on election day the shops close at four o'clock so that employees get the three full hours to which they are entitled by virtue of section 47 of the Canada Elections Act. Actually, the employer is giving his employees only a half hour or an hour, depending upon what time the particular shop is normally closed down; but at any rate, that pattern seems to have established itself and is reasonably satisfactory so far as general elections are concerned because of the fact that they usually take place when daylight saving time is in effect.
However, Mr. Speaker, when a by-election is called, particularly when a by-election is held during the winter season, during the period of the year when daylight saving time is not in effect, actually two problems arise. In the first place, since standard time is in effect it means that the polls do close at six o'clock instead of at seven o'clock. That means that if an employer is going to let his employees off in time to get the full three hours he has to let them off at three o'clock in order to meet the requirements of section 47.
Well, employers do not go around looking for ways to let employees off even for the exercise of the franchise; but it becomes a particular problem in by-elections, particularly when they take place in an urban area, because working in a plant or in a factory will be a few employees who live in the constituency where the by-election is held, whereas the majority of the employees probably live in other constituencies in that same area, and in those other constituencies a byelection is not being held. That applies particularly when a by-election is held in an urban area like Toronto, Montreal, Winnipeg or Vancouver. As a result of that situation employees are a little reluctant to ask for

time off when they know their fellow employees cannot make the same request, and employers put up a certain amount of resistance to it as well.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that this problem could easily be solved if a provision such as is proposed in Bill No. 205 were written into the Canada Elections Act. The proposal is simply that during the period when daylight saving time is not in effect, in the case of a by-election, the polls should remain open until seven o'clock in the evening. If that were done then we would have the same situation that applies in most general elections. Section 47 could be met by letting employees off at four o'clock rather than having to let them off at three o'clock in the afternoon. To be sure, the employees would rather be off at three o'clock than at four o'clock, but the fact is that in by-elections they do not get off at all in many instances. Reluctance and resistance go together, and the result is that the rights granted under section 47 of the Canada Elections Act are not enjoyed by those voting in a by-election.
It might be argued by anyone who sought to oppose this bill that provisions such as these should be made to apply to general elections as well as by-elections. I would say, Mr. Speaker, if it were at all the rule for general elections to be held in the winter months the change should perhaps be made to apply to general elections as well as byelections, but as I have already pointed out six out of the last seven general elections in this country have been held during the months when daylight saving time was in effect and the chances are the same will be the case for the next election year.
It might also be contended that in making special provision for a by-election one is paying too much attention to the exceptions rather than the rule, since after all the act is for general elections rather than by-elections. In answer to that I would point out that the Canada Elections Act already contains a number of special provisions that apply to by-elections but do not apply to general elections. One or two occur to me immediately. First of all, the period of time during which the enumerating takes place is two weeks shorter in the case of a by-election than it is in the case of a general election. Indeed, there are even some other provisions with regard to the lists of electors that apply to by-elections which are different from those which apply in the case of a general election.
There is also a special provision in the section of the act as to what would happen if the Monday chosen for an election turned out to be a holiday. In the case of a general election that holiday would have to be a national holiday before the result would be
Canada Elections Act
the putting off of the election until Tuesday, but in the case of a by-election regard is had as to whether the holiday is national or provincial in character.
I need not go into any further detail on that. I just mention those one or two things to point out that the act already contains a number of provisions that are exclusively for by-elections as distinct from general elections. Indeed, the definition section defines general election and it defines by-election, and there are differences running through the act. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, it seems to me it is not only a simple request but it is a very justifiable one. The suggestion that a change like this be made, as a matter of fact, has come out of the experience of certain byelections that were held recently, when a number of employees found they could not get to the polls by six o'clock for the very reason I have given; namely, that it was difficult to get sufficient time off. In fact there were many people, so I am told, in one recent by-election who did not get to the polls because they had become accustomed to the idea of federal elections closing for all practical purposes at seven o'clock because of the fact that general elections are usually held when daylight saving time is in effect.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that this is an extremely reasonable and sensible suggestion to put forward, and I hope it will be given consideration by the house. I remind hon. members again that when we are dealing with the Canada Elections Act we are dealing with something that is in a particular way not the property of the government nor even the property of parliament. In a particular way it is the property of the people of Canada. It seems to me that on as sensible and rational a basis as we can, we should make it an act that will make possible the fullest exercise of the franchise not only at general elections but at by-elections as well.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I have pleasure in commending the provisions of Bill No. 205 to the house.

Mr. Speaker, I have listened with great interest to the remarks made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) in introducing this measure on behalf of the late Joseph Noseworthy, who was the original sponsor of this bill. I think I may take advantage of this opportunity to again express sincere sympathy on behalf of us all. When we heard during the last Easter recess of the death of the late Joseph Noseworthy a sense of great loss was felt by every hon. member of this house.
The fact that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has accepted the sponsorship

of this bill is a further demonstration of his interest in the Canada Elections Act, because the hon. member already has on the order paper another bill which also provides suggested amendments to this act.
I must say first of all that I am in agreement with what the hon. member said at the conclusion of his remarks, namely that the Canada Elections Act is not the property of the government. It is a matter which belongs not only to parliament itself but to every hon. member of this house. For this reason I would think an amendment such as the one which is now being proposed, even if it is very simple, should first of all receive the attention of the members of the house in committee when the time comes for the committee on privileges and elections to meet and study the revision of the act. On the other hand, and I do not think I am mistaken in saying this, the subject matter of this amendment has never been discussed by the members of the committee on privileges and elections to my knowledge. Possibly it has not been discussed because it does not appear, to me at least, to be a necessary remedy.
Under the act as it now stands there is a very clear provision which applies both to general elections and by-elections. In section 47 to which my hon. friend referred are to be found both the obligation and the right of the employer and the employee. The section provides that three consecutive hours will be made available by the employer to the employee in order to exercise his right to vote. These hours must be consecutive. This applies to both general elections and by-elections. The section also provides that:
... no employer shall make any deduction from the pay of any such employee nor impose upon or exact from him any penalty by reason of absence from his work during such consecutive hours.
In subsection 3 of section 47 is provided a penalty for the employer who does not allow the employee the benefit of three consecutive hours in which to exercise his right to vote.
I am afraid I did not understand very clearly the distinction the hon. member attempted to make between a general election and a by-election. It seems to me the fact that general elections have been held in the last four or five instances during that period of the year when daylight saving time is in effect is not a reason for making a distinction between the two. In other words the voter has as much right to vote in a by-election as he has in a general election, and the employer must carry out his duty in both cases.
To say that in urban districts it may be difficult in some cases for the employer to make these hours available to the employees to me is not enough to justify the amendment


of the act to cover by-elections only. Surely the time elapsing between nomination day and polling day, a period of 14 days, should be sufficient for the employer and employee to discuss arrangements so the employee may be allowed time off as provided by the act in which to exercise his right to vote. A by-election in itself creates interest, and that should be enough to make the employer aware that among his employees there are one, two or possibly a greater number who have the right to vote and who should have time off. Arrangements can be made so the employee will have the benefit of the three consecutive hours provided by the act.
It is the duty of the employee who wants to vote to see to it that he is given the necessary time in which to exercise his right to vote. I do not think my hon. friend will contradict me on that. If the employee does not make the necessary arrangements with his employer, if he does not want to take advantage of the fact that he is entitled to three hours and that the employer must make those hours available to him, I do not think he will exercise his right to vote simply because the act is amended to give him an additional hour on polling day.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND HOURS OF POLLING
speechtext: What about the situation where 25 per cent of the employees in a certain plant are entitled to vote in a by-election and the remaining 75 per cent are not? The act is quite clear that the 25 per cent must be given the right to vote, but is it not so that the 75 per cent would have no protection under the act? The employer might decide that as 25 per cent of his employees were going to be away for part of the day he might just as well close down his plant, and the 75 per cent of the employees would lose a certain amount of pay and would have no recourse under the act.

My hon. friend has given an example. In a general election 100 per cent of the employees would most likely have the right to vote and the employer must make it possible for them to vote on polling day. Under such conditions he makes arrangements so there will not be too great a disruption in his operations. He arranges for his employees to go and vote without disrupting the whole operation.
To my mind the extending of the period by one hour in the case of by-elections will not create any more interest on the part of the employer or employee. If the employee is not convinced that he should exercise his right to vote, I do not think that giving him another hour on polling day will change his mind.

Does the minister not realize that that is precisely where there may be a distinction? We want the polls to close at seven o'clock in by-elections just as they do in general elections. The effect of the law is to make a distinction. When by-elections are held in the wintertime the polls close at six o'clock, but in the case of general elections they usually close at seven o'clock.

elections will always be held when daylight saving time is in operation, but a general election might be held in the wintertime and then we would have amended the act to cover by-elections only and would find ourselves faced with the situation where in a general election you would have the same inconvenience, if the inconvenience exists. In other words, I submit that both general elections and by-elections should be covered. However, I do not say that should be done, because I feel that it would not create any interest for an employee who had decided not to vote by merely extending the time for voting by one hour.
